desc: Savage, overdriven proto-punk with James Williamson's slashing guitar, controversially mixed by David Bowie.
Live double album of droning, pulsing space rock interspersed with science-fiction poetry recitations.
Percussion-heavy instrumental funk whose breaks, especially Apache, became foundational to early hip hop.
Wings' melodic, ambitious album recorded largely in Lagos, Nigeria, with escape-themed songs.
Lou Reed's orchestrated rock opera tracing a doomed, abusive relationship in divided Berlin.
Faust's fourth album mixing long motorik drones, whimsical songs and studio collage, opening with Krautrock.
John Cale's lushly orchestrated, literate pop songs, backed by members of Little Feat.
Genesis's intricate prog suites exploring English identity and commercialism, featuring Firth of Fifth.
John Martyn's slurred, jazzy folk with echo-treated guitar and Danny Thompson's upright bass.
Sloppy, glammed-up rock and roll debut produced by Todd Rundgren, an influence on punk.
Steely Dan's second album, with extended guitar solos and jazz-inflected, ironic songwriting.
Bowie's American-tour-inspired glam record, noted for Mike Garson's avant-garde piano.
Rundgren's restless one-man studio collage of short song fragments, soul medleys and electronic experiments.
Alice Cooper's lurid, Bob Ezrin-produced hard rock theatre including No More Mr. Nice Guy.
Can's airy, aquatic grooves with Damo Suzuki's murmured vocals, their last album with him.
Elton John and Bernie Taupin's sprawling double album of ballads, rockers and Hollywood nostalgia.
Stevie Wonder, largely playing everything himself, addresses drugs, racism and faith over synth-driven funk.
King Crimson's new lineup pairs violin and heavy guitar with Jamie Muir's unusual percussion.
Marvin Gaye's lush, intimate soul album devoted to love and desire.
Lynyrd Skynyrd's three-guitar debut, featuring Simple Man and the extended Free Bird.
Mike Oldfield's multi-tracked instrumental suite, playing most instruments himself; its opening was used in The Exorcist.
Herbie Hancock's synth-driven jazz-funk record featuring Chameleon and a reworked Watermelon Man.
Seamless concept album about time, money and madness, with pioneering studio effects and sound collage.
Gram Parsons' posthumously released album, built on close harmonies with Emmylou Harris.
George Jones sings lavish, Billy Sherrill-produced country ballads of lost love and regret.
Clapton's relaxed comeback album recorded in Miami, including his cover of I Shot the Sheriff.
Richard and Linda Thompson's debut duo album of dark, wry songs with traditional English folk flavour.
Van Morrison's live double album with the Caledonia Soul Orchestra, mixing originals and R&B covers.
Sparks' breakthrough of operatic falsetto and frenzied, witty glam pop, featuring This Town Ain't Big Enough.
Queen's dense, layered album split into a White Side and Black Side of fantasy-themed songs.
Queen's eclectic third album mixing heavy rock, vaudeville and early speed metal, including Killer Queen.
Former Byrd Gene Clark's expansive, richly produced album blending country, gospel and soul.
Supertramp's polished concept album on alienation and mental breakdown, featuring School and Dreamer.
Randy Newman's orchestral song cycle examining the American South through ironic character portraits.
10cc's inventive, genre-hopping pop full of parody and studio craft, including The Wall Street Shuffle.
Gil Scott-Heron and Brian Jackson's sparse, jazzy soul of social commentary, including The Bottle.
Roxy Music's fourth album of suave, edgy art rock, including Thrill of It All.
Stevie Wonder's reflective follow-up to Innervisions, featuring Boogie On Reggae Woman and You Haven't Done Nothin'.
Eno's first solo album of skewed, noisy glam pop with treated guitars from Robert Fripp and Phil Manzanera.
Shuggie Otis's largely self-played psychedelic soul with early drum machine, later rediscovered.
Robert Wyatt's first album after a fall left him paraplegic; aquatic, tender and abstract.
Steely Dan's concise jazz-pop songs, including Rikki Don't Lose That Number and a Duke Ellington cover.
Supergroup's debut of straightforward, bluesy hard rock led by Paul Rodgers' vocals.
Joni Mitchell's polished, jazz-tinged pop with L.A. Express, including Help Me and Free Man in Paris.
First Wailers album without Tosh and Bunny, featuring No Woman, No Cry and the I Threes.
Neil Young's loose, despairing post-fame album, part of his informal Ditch trilogy.
Tangerine Dream's early sequencer-driven synth soundscapes, a cornerstone of Berlin School electronic music.
Peter Gabriel's final Genesis album, a surreal double-album story about a Puerto Rican youth in New York.
Kraftwerk's breakthrough, its 22-minute title track evoking a motorway drive through synthesizers.
Emmylou Harris's major-label debut of carefully chosen covers sung in her clear, aching voice.
Willie Nelson's stripped-down concept album about a fugitive preacher, including Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain.
Bob Dylan's raw, intimate songs of failed love, including Tangled Up in Blue.
Keith Jarrett's fully improvised solo piano concert in Cologne, a bestselling solo jazz recording.
Dion's dark, slow, Phil Spector-produced album of dense, echoing Wall of Sound ballads.
Aerosmith's breakthrough with riff-driven hard rock including Walk This Way and Sweet Emotion.
Queen's extravagant, genre-spanning album, including the operatic multi-section Bohemian Rhapsody.
Burning Spear's Rastafarian tribute to Marcus Garvey over deep, slow roots reggae grooves.
Parliament's Afrofuturist funk concept album, with Bernie Worrell's synths and the Horny Horns, including Give Up the Funk.
Earth, Wind & Fire's breakthrough with Shining Star, combining soul, funk and jazz arrangements.
Springsteen's widescreen rock about escape and youthful longing, with Clarence Clemons' saxophone.
The Dictators' jokey, loud debut of pop-culture-obsessed rock, an early precursor of New York punk.
Bowie's Philadelphia-recorded soul album, including Fame, co-written with John Lennon.
Curtis Mayfield's understated, bleak soul album on poverty and racism in 1970s America.
Eno's blend of short instrumentals and gentle songs, bridging art pop and his later ambient work.
Patti Smith's debut fusing Beat-style poetry with raw rock, produced by John Cale.
Tom Waits' live studio set of beat-style monologues and lounge jazz before a small audience.
Joni Mitchell's jazz-leaning songs on suburban life and gender, with experimental African drum sampling.
Neil Young's loose, ragged wake for two friends lost to heroin, recorded mostly in 1973.
NEU!'s third album, split between ambient pieces and pounding proto-punk such as Hero.
Led Zeppelin's sprawling double album, including Kashmir and In My Time of Dying.
Pink Floyd's tribute to Syd Barrett and critique of the music industry, featuring Shine On You Crazy Diamond.
The Eagles' polished look at California excess, known for the title track's dual-guitar coda.
Aerosmith's heavier, dirtier follow-up to Toys in the Attic, including Back in the Saddle.
Joan Armatrading's Glyn Johns-produced album of rich-voiced, emotionally direct songs, including Love and Affection.
Stevie Wonder's expansive double album of soul and funk, including Sir Duke and Isn't She Lovely.
Peter Frampton's bestselling live double album, known for talk box solos on Show Me the Way.
KISS's Bob Ezrin-produced studio album, including Detroit Rock City and the ballad Beth.
Tom Petty's tight debut of jangling, Byrds-influenced rock, including American Girl and Breakdown.
ABBA's highly polished pop album, including Dancing Queen, Money Money Money and Knowing Me, Knowing You.
Peter Tosh's solo debut and pro-marijuana title track, with relaxed, militant roots reggae.
Jorge Ben's electrified fusion of samba, funk and African rhythms, including Taj Mahal.
Tom Scholz's meticulously home-produced debut of layered guitars, including More Than a Feeling.
Joni Mitchell's travelogue songs of solitude and the road, shaped by Jaco Pastorius's fretless bass.
Bowie's Thin White Duke album, blending funk, soul and European electronic influence on extended tracks.
Jonathan Richman's Velvet Underground-influenced demos, including Roadrunner and Pablo Picasso, released years after recording.
Jean-Michel Jarre's home-studio synthesizer suite in six parts, a major commercial electronic success.
Fourteen short, loud, minimal songs in under 30 minutes that helped define punk rock.
Rush's dystopian sci-fi concept, its side-long title suite inspired by Ayn Rand.
Fela Kuti's satirical attack on Nigerian soldiers over long, driving Afrobeat grooves.
Simon Jeffes' quirky chamber ensemble mixing folk, minimalism and world music into gentle instrumentals.
Elvis Costello's debut of sharp, literate songs, backed by Clover, including Alison and Watching the Detectives.
Television's interlocking twin-guitar epics from Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd on the CBGB scene.
Meat Loaf and Jim Steinman's operatic, Rundgren-produced teenage melodramas built on Springsteen-style grandeur.
ELO's lavish double album of orchestral pop, including Mr. Blue Sky.
Beach Boys drummer Dennis Wilson's gravelly-voiced solo album of lush, wounded songs.
Iggy Pop's upbeat Bowie collaboration, including the title track and The Passenger.
Peter Gabriel's first solo album after Genesis, produced by Bob Ezrin, including Solsbury Hill.
Alan Vega and Martin Rev's minimal duo of crude drum machine, synth and echoing vocals, including Frankie Teardrop.
Iggy Pop's Bowie-produced album of mechanical, dark grooves, including China Girl and Nightclubbing.
Steely Dan's immaculately produced jazz-rock album with session virtuosos, including Peg and Deacon Blues.
Eno's album of angular art rock songs giving way to quiet, reflective pieces on its second side.
Recorded in London exile, with Jamming, One Love and Three Little Birds.
Ian Dury's music-hall-tinged pub rock with the Blockheads, full of London characters and wordplay.
Wire's debut of 21 brief, stripped-down punk songs, many under two minutes.
The Stranglers' debut of swirling organ and prominent bass, including Peaches and Hanging Around.
Talking Heads' debut of jittery, minimal art-punk songs, including Psycho Killer.
Kraftwerk's European travel concept with metallic rhythms, influential on hip hop and electro.
Bowie's Berlin album with Eno and Fripp, pairing the anthemic title track with instrumental pieces.
Muddy Waters' late-career comeback produced by Johnny Winter, with James Cotton's harmonica, recorded loosely and loud.
John Martyn's spacious, echo-laden album with Lee Perry and Steve Winwood contributions, including Small Hours.
The Clash's raw, politically charged debut, including White Riot and a cover of Police and Thieves.
Weather Report's most popular album, with Zawinul's synths and Jaco Pastorius's bass, including Birdland.
The Sex Pistols' only studio album, with layered guitars and provocative songs like God Save the Queen.
Billy Joel's Phil Ramone-produced breakthrough, including Just the Way You Are and Scenes from an Italian Restaurant.
Bowie's fragmented song side and ambient instrumental side, with heavily processed drums.
Fleetwood Mac's polished songs written amid the band's breakups, including Go Your Own Way and Dreams.
Joe Ely's Texas honky tonk with accordion and steel guitar, mixing Butch Hancock songs and originals.
The Only Ones' debut, led by Peter Perrett's drawling vocals, including Another Girl, Another Planet.
Springsteen's leaner, darker record about working-class struggle, including Badlands and The Promised Land.
Pere Ubu's debut combining avant-garde synth noise and garage rock under David Thomas's yelps.
Elvis Costello's first album with the Attractions, driven by Steve Nieve's organ, including Pump It Up.
Willie Colon and Ruben Blades' bestselling salsa album with socially conscious lyrics, including Pedro Navaja.
Siouxsie and the Banshees' stark, angular debut, including Jigsaw Feeling and a Helter Skelter cover.
R.D. Burman's soundtrack for the heist film Shalimar, mixing Hindi film song with disco and funk.
The Adverts' only major album of punk songs by T.V. Smith, including One Chord Wonders.
Pere Ubu's denser second album of murky, dub-influenced industrial art punk.
Marvin Gaye's double album about his divorce from Anna Gordy, with royalties owed in the settlement.
Blondie's Mike Chapman-produced new wave pop album, including Heart of Glass and Hanging on the Telephone.
Willie Nelson's Booker T. Jones-produced collection of pop standards, including Georgia on My Mind.
The Saints' second album, adding brass to their punk sound, including Know Your Product.
The Jam's Kinks-influenced album of English character songs, including Down in the Tube Station at Midnight.
Buzzcocks' debut of fast, melodic punk about love and frustration, produced by Martin Hannett.
Chic's tight, elegant disco album led by Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards, including Le Freak.
Dire Straits' sparse debut showcasing Mark Knopfler's fingerpicked guitar, including Sultans of Swing.
The Residents' warped short songs and twisted vocals, compiling an EP and a single.
Talking Heads' first Eno collaboration, adding funk rhythms, including a cover of Take Me to the River.
Funkadelic's bestselling album, with its long title-track groove and rock-leaning P-Funk jams.
X-Ray Spex's only album, with Poly Styrene's shrill vocals and saxophone critiquing consumerism.
